issues.legal_issue: A tenant who refuses a properly sent registered postal notice demanding rent may be imputed with knowledge of the notice’s contents.
material_facts: The landlords sent a registered notice demanding rent arrears and seeking eviction to the tenant.
The postman testified that he tendered the notice to the tenant, who refused to accept it, and the lower appellate court accepted that evidence.
The tenant did not comply with the demand in the notice.
issues.conclusion: The refusal constituted effective service, and the tenant was imputed with knowledge of the notice’s contents; his failure to comply with the demand could therefore amount to willful default.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 and 114, Illustration (f), of the Indian Evidence Act support rebuttable presumptions of proper or effective postal service. Where service is proved by refusal, those presumptions permit the addressee to be imputed with knowledge of the communication’s contents; opening or reading the envelope is unnecessary. The Court approved Shri Nath v. Smt. Saraswati Devi Jaiswal, Fanni Lal v. Smt. Chironja, Ganga Ram v. Smt. Phulwati, and Kodali Bapayya v. Yadavalli Venkataratnam, and referred to Harihar Banerji v. Ramshashi Roy; it explained and dissented from Vaman Vithal Kulkarni v. Khanderao Ram Rao Sholapurkar and held Mahboob Bi v. Alvala Lachmiah inapplicable.

rule.if: rent_default_eviction_proceeding and properly_addressed_registered_notice and notice_tendered_and_refused and not presumption_rebutted

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction on the basis of a tenant’s failure to pay rent after a demand notice.
predicates.properly_addressed_registered_notice: The landlord sent the notice by registered post to the tenant at a proper address.
predicates.notice_tendered_and_refused: The postal carrier tendered the notice to the tenant, and the tenant refused to accept it.
predicates.presumption_rebutted: Evidence established that the postal communication was not effectively served or that the presumption of service was otherwise displaced.

issues.definition: In a rent-default eviction proceeding, when a properly addressed registered notice is tendered and refused and the presumption of service is not rebutted, the notice is treated as effectively served with its contents known.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord need not obtain the District Magistrate’s permission to sue for eviction on a ground expressly listed among the statutory exceptions to that permission requirement.
material_facts: The landlords sued for eviction on the ground that the tenant had willfully failed to pay rent within the required period after service of a demand notice.
The eviction ground was one of the grounds listed as an exception to the permission requirement.
The landlords had not obtained the District Magistrate’s permission before filing the suit.
issues.conclusion: The suit was maintainable without the District Magistrate’s permission because it was brought on a specified statutory ground.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the U.P. Cantonment (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1952 requires permission for an eviction suit based on a ground other than those specified in clauses (a) to (f), but not for a suit based on one of those specified grounds. The Court followed Bhagwan Dass v. Paras Nath, which interpreted the materially similar provision in section 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947.

predicates.eviction_suit_under_cantonment_rent_cont: A landlord brought an eviction suit governed by a rent-control law applicable to cantonment premises.
predicates.eviction_ground_in_listed_exceptions: The landlord relied on a ground that the law expressly lists as an exception to the requirement for prior permission.

issues.definition: When an eviction suit governed by a cantonment rent-control law relies on a ground listed as an exception, prior permission from the designated authority is not required.

issues.legal_issue: The governing rent-control law for premises subject to the cantonment regime is the central cantonment rent-control law rather than the other regional rent-control laws discussed in the judgment.
material_facts: The premises were within a cantonment and were governed at all material times by the central cantonment rent-control law.
The lower courts dealt with the dispute under that law.
issues.conclusion: The matter was governed by the U.P. Cantonment (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1952, not by the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 or the later U.P. (Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the governing law was the central cantonment rent-control enactment because the premises were governed by that enactment; the other regional enactments did not govern the dispute.

predicates.premises_governed_by_cantonment_rent_con: The premises fall within and are governed by the rent-control regime applicable to cantonment premises.
predicates.rent_control_dispute: The dispute concerns rights or remedies arising from a tenancy of those premises.

issues.definition: When a rent-control dispute concerns premises governed by the cantonment regime, that regime governs the dispute.
